passages.title: Molly Whuppie and the Giant
passages.text:
The youngest of the three strange lassies was called Molly Whuppie, and she was very clever. She noticed that before they went to bed the giant put straw ropes round her neck and her sisters', and round his own lassies' necks he put gold chains. So Molly took care and did not fall asleep, but waited till she was sure every one was sleeping sound. Then she slipped out of the bed, and took the straw ropes off her own and her sisters' necks, and took the gold chains off the giant's lassies. She then put the straw ropes on the giant's lassies and the gold on herself and her sisters, and lay down.

And in the middle of the night up rose the giant, armed with a great club, and felt for the necks with the straw. It was dark. He took his own lassies out of bed on to the floor, and battered them until they were dead, and then lay down again, thinking he had managed fine. Molly thought it time she and her sisters were out of that, so she wakened them and told them to be quiet, and they slipped out of the house. They all got out safe, and they ran and ran, and never stopped until morning, when they saw a grand house before them. It turned out to be a king's house: so Molly went in, and told her story to the king. He said: "Well, Molly, you are a clever girl, and you have managed well; but, if you would manage better, and go back, and steal the giant's sword that hangs on the back of his bed, I would give your eldest sister my eldest son to marry." Molly said she would try.

So she went back, and managed to slip into the giant's house, and crept in below the bed. The giant came home, and ate up a great supper, and went to bed. Molly waited until he was snoring, and she crept out, and reached over the giant and got down the sword; but just as she got it out over the bed it gave a rattle, and up jumped the giant, and Molly ran out at the door and the sword with her; and she ran, and he ran, till they came to the "Bridge of one hair"; and she got over, but he couldn't, and he says, "Woe worth ye, Molly Whuppie! never ye come again." And she says "Twice yet, carle," quoth she, "I'll come to Spain." So Molly took the sword to the king, and her sister was married to his son.

Well, the king he says: "Ye've managed well, Molly; but if ye would manage better, and steal the purse that lies below the giant's pillow, I would marry your second sister to my second son." And Molly said she would try. So she set out for the giant's house, and slipped in, and hid again below the bed, and waited till the giant had eaten his supper, and was snoring sound asleep. She slipped out, and slipped her hand below the pillow, and got out the purse; but just as she was going out the giant wakened, and ran after her; and she ran, and he ran, till they came to the "Bridge of one hair," and she got over, but he couldn't, and he said, "Woe worth ye, Molly Whuppie! never you come again." "Once yet, carle," quoth she, "I'll come to Spain." So Molly took the purse to the king, and her second sister was married to the king's second son.
passages.source_note: Public domain: from English Fairy Tales by Joseph Jacobs (1890). Straight quotation marks substituted for typographic ones.

questions.stem: What does the opening sentence suggest about Molly Whuppie's mind?

options.text: She was easily frightened by the dark
She was sharp-witted and quick to notice things
She was forgetful and often careless
She was lazy and slow to act
She was cheerful but rather foolish

questions.explanation: The passage says she 'was very clever' and immediately shows her noticing a detail others missed, so 'sharp-witted' fits.

questions.stem: Round whose necks did the giant put gold chains?

options.text: Round Molly and her sisters' necks
Round the necks of everyone in the bed
Round nobody's neck that night
Round his own lassies' necks
Round the king's daughters' necks

questions.explanation: The text states the giant 'round his own lassies' necks he put gold chains', while the strangers got straw ropes.

questions.stem: What is the main job of the paragraph beginning 'And in the middle of the night'?

options.text: To describe the king's grand house in detail
To explain the rules of the Bridge of one hair
To introduce the three sisters for the first time
To list the treasures the giant owns
To show the giant's trick backfiring and the escape that follows

questions.explanation: That paragraph shows the giant killing his own lassies by mistake and Molly leading her sisters out of the house, so its job is to turn the swap into the escape.

questions.stem: The giant twice warns 'never ye come again', yet Molly replies 'Twice yet, carle' — 'I'll come to Spain' — and later 'Once yet'. Why does the author give her this counting reply?

options.text: To prove Molly has lost count of her own visits
To suggest Molly is frightened of coming back
To warn the reader that further returns are promised, not yet finished
To explain why the giant lives so near to Spain
To show that Molly has decided to stop visiting the giant

questions.explanation: Her reply names a shrinking count -- 'Twice yet' then 'Once yet' -- against the giant's 'never ye come again', so it hints to the reader that more visits are still to come and the story is not over.

questions.stem: In 'battered them until they were dead', which meaning does the word 'battered' carry here?

options.text: struck heavily and repeatedly
coated in flour and fried
wrapped up warmly
scolded with angry words
carried gently away

questions.explanation: Here 'battered' describes the giant striking with his great club until his lassies were dead, so it means struck heavily and repeatedly.

questions.stem: What effect does the repetition in 'they ran and ran, and never stopped until morning' create?

options.text: It suggests the sisters are moving very slowly
It makes the flight feel long and breathless
It shows the sisters keep changing direction
It proves the giant is chasing close behind
It tells us exactly how far they travelled

questions.explanation: Doubling 'ran' stretches the action out, giving a sense of a long, tiring, breathless escape lasting all night.

questions.stem: According to the text, why did the giant attack his own lassies by mistake?

options.text: Because they had stolen his gold chains
Because Molly had woken him with a noise
Because his wife pointed to the wrong bed
Because they were snoring too loudly
Because he felt for the necks with the straw in the dark

questions.explanation: The text says he 'felt for the necks with the straw' and 'It was dark', so, after Molly's swap, the straw led him to his own daughters.

questions.stem: What does 'It was dark' help us understand about the giant's mistake?

options.text: That it was already the following morning
That the fire had been left burning brightly
That he could not see and had to judge by touch alone
That the giant had poor hearing
That the sisters had hidden under the floor

questions.explanation: The short sentence tells us he could not see; relying on touch, he trusted the straw ropes and so struck the wrong bed.

questions.stem: Where does the king say the giant's sword hangs?

options.text: Below the giant's pillow
On the back of his bed
Over the fire in the kitchen
On the king's own wall
Beside the Bridge of one hair

questions.explanation: The king asks Molly to 'steal the giant's sword that hangs on the back of his bed'.

questions.stem: In the phrase 'a grand house before them', which word is an adjective?

options.text: house
before
grand
them
a

questions.explanation: 'grand' describes the noun 'house', telling us what kind of house it is, so it is an adjective.

questions.stem: When 'Molly said she would try', what does this show about her response to the king?

options.text: She flatly refused the dangerous errand
She demanded gold before she would move
She asked her sisters to go instead
She pretended she had not heard him
She agreed to make the dangerous attempt he asked for

questions.explanation: 'she would try' is a quiet agreement to attempt the task, showing she takes on the challenge rather than turning it down.

questions.stem: How does the king's line 'you are a clever girl, and you have managed well' come across?

options.text: Bitter and threatening
Bored and dismissive
Warmly approving, yet ready to ask for more
Frightened and pleading
Mocking and unkind

questions.explanation: The praise is genuine ('clever girl'), but he at once pairs it with a fresh demand, so the tone is approving while still pressing her on.

questions.stem: Which phrase best shows that Molly plans her theft coolly rather than acting on impulse?

options.text: 'took care and did not fall asleep'
'up rose the giant'
'up jumped the giant'
'told her story to the king'
'ate up a great supper'

questions.explanation: The line 'took care and did not fall asleep' shows Molly deliberately staying awake to watch, which is careful planning rather than a rash act.

questions.stem: In the sword adventure, which happens FIRST?

options.text: The sword gives a rattle over the bed
Molly creeps in below the bed
The giant reaches the Bridge of one hair
Molly hands the sword to the king
The giant eats up a great supper and then Molly grabs the blade

questions.explanation: The order runs: she slips in and 'crept in below the bed', then the giant sups and sleeps, then the rattle, then the chase to the bridge, then the delivery. Creeping below the bed comes first.

questions.stem: The name 'Bridge of one hair' works mainly by

options.text: comparing the bridge to a person using 'like'
copying a real sound the bridge makes
giving the bridge human feelings
repeating the same first letter for effect
exaggeration that pictures an impossibly thin crossing

questions.explanation: A bridge as narrow as a single hair is a deliberate exaggeration (hyperbole), picturing a crossing almost too thin to be real.

questions.stem: After Molly brought the sword to the king, what happened to one of her sisters?

options.text: She was sent back to the wood
She was given the giant's gold chains
She became the giant's servant
She ran away over the bridge
She was married to the king's son

questions.explanation: The text ends the sword episode with 'her sister was married to his son'.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the detail that the sword 'gave a rattle'?

options.text: To provide the sudden noise that wakes the giant and starts the chase
To show the sword is broken and useless
To prove the giant is already awake
To describe how heavy the sword is
To remind us the room is crowded

questions.explanation: The rattle is the trigger: it is the noise that makes the giant jump up, so the detail is needed to launch the chase.

questions.stem: The author writes that Molly 'crept out' instead of using a plainer word for moving. Which idea does 'crept' add?

options.text: That she moved quietly and secretly
That she moved boldly and loudly
That she moved cheerfully and quickly
That she moved clumsily and by accident
That she moved sadly and slowly

questions.explanation: 'crept' carries a sense of quiet, secret movement, which 'walked' would not, fitting her need not to wake the giant.

questions.stem: Why does the king keep asking Molly to steal the giant's belongings?

options.text: Because he is testing whether she will lie to him
Because he has no soldiers of his own left
Because the giant is a friend he wishes to tease
Because he wants to weaken the giant while rewarding Molly's daring
Because he needs money to feed his sons

questions.explanation: Each errand strips the giant of something and each success earns a marriage, so the king is both robbing the giant and rewarding Molly's boldness.

questions.stem: Across this excerpt, how is the story shaped?

options.text: It circles back to end exactly where it began
It drifts with no clear order of events
It tells the same single event from two viewpoints
It repeats a rising pattern of task, theft and reward
It moves backwards from the ending to the start

questions.explanation: The excerpt sets a task, shows a daring theft and a chase, then a reward, and repeats this shape for the sword and again for the purse.

questions.stem: In 'Molly waited until he was snoring', what job does the word 'snoring' do?

options.text: It names a person or thing
It joins two sentences together
It describes an action the giant is doing
It stands in place of a noun
It shows where something happens

questions.explanation: 'was snoring' tells us the action the giant is performing, so 'snoring' works as a verb (part of the verb phrase) here.

questions.stem: Which phrase from the passage is an example of alliteration?

options.text: 'sure every one was sleeping sound'
'slipped her hand below the pillow'
'took the gold chains'
'a great club'
'out at the door'

questions.explanation: 'sleeping sound' repeats the opening 's' sound (echoed by 'sure'), which is alliteration.

questions.stem: In 'just as she was going out the giant wakened', 'wakened' means the giant

options.text: fell into a deep sleep
stood guard at the door
began to snore
woke up
cried out in pain

questions.explanation: 'wakened' here means woke up: he rouses from sleep just as she is leaving, which is why he runs after her.

questions.stem: Where does the king say the purse lies?

options.text: On the back of the giant's bed
Inside the giant's supper pot
Over the Bridge of one hair
Below the giant's pillow
In the king's own house

questions.explanation: The king asks Molly to 'steal the purse that lies below the giant's pillow'.

questions.stem: What does 'thinking he had managed fine' reveal about the giant?

options.text: He is careful and rarely makes mistakes
He wrongly believes he has succeeded
He knows at once that he has been tricked
He is worried he has harmed the wrong girls
He plans to chase Molly straight away

questions.explanation: He lies down 'thinking he had managed fine', so he is sure of a success he has not actually had -- he has been fooled.
